title: Corporate Bonds & Debentures
subtitle: Debt securities issued by Indian corporations and public sector enterprises
summary: Corporate bonds allow retail investors to lend directly to blue-chip corporations and NBFCs in exchange for regular, higher interest coupon payouts than traditional bank deposits.

sources.name: SEBI Debt Market Regulations & Operational Framework
Income Tax Act, Section 193 (TDS on Debentures)

disclaimer: Educational information only. Not investment advice. TradeOne is not a SEBI-registered investment adviser. Rules, taxes and yields change; verify with official sources.

sections.title: What are Corporate Bonds?
sections.content: When corporations need capital to build factories, expand retail operations, or fund working capital, they can borrow from banks, issue equity shares, or issue debt bonds (Non-Convertible Debentures, or NCDs). As a bondholder, you are a creditor of the company, not a shareholder.
sections.analogy: Imagine lending money to a reputable company like Tata Capital or NHAI. In exchange for your loan, they sign a legal covenant to pay you a specified coupon rate every year and return your full principal on a stated maturity date, irrespective of whether company share price moves up or down.

sections.title: How Investors Earn from Corporate Bonds
points: Fixed Coupon Income: Paid annually, semi-annually, or monthly according to bond terms.
Maturity Par Value: 100% repayment of face value upon maturity.
Secondary Trading Gains: Buying bonds at a discount on the exchange or OBPP platform and holding to par or selling as credit ratings improve.

sections.title: What are the Risks?
sections.content: Unlike sovereign debt, corporate bonds entail credit and default risk:
points: Credit / Default Risk: The risk that the borrowing company faces financial distress and fails to pay coupons or principal. Always check external credit ratings (CRISIL, ICRA, CARE, India Ratings).
Rating Downgrade Risk: If a bond is downgraded from AAA to AA or BBB, its market price drops immediately on the secondary market.
Liquidity Risk: Many corporate debentures trade infrequently on exchange order books, making quick exits challenging without price concessions.

sections.title: Who Often Considers Corporate Bonds?
sections.content: Investors seeking steady fixed yields (historically 8% to 10% on AA/AAA rated issues) higher than bank fixed deposits, who are comfortable taking measured corporate credit risk.

sections.title: Worked Example (Sample Illustration)
sections.content: An investor purchases 10 units of an AAA-rated corporate bond with ₹10,000 face value and 8.50% annual coupon (Total investment: ₹1,00,000).
details: Annual coupon interest: 8.50% of ₹1,00,000 = ₹8,500 credited annually.
At maturity, the company repays the ₹1,00,000 principal in full (assuming no default).

sections.title: Tax Overview in Plain English
sections.content: Tax implications of corporate debt instruments:
points: Coupon (Interest) Income: Added to your gross total income and taxed at your marginal slab rate.
TDS: 10% TDS is deducted under Section 193 on interest from listed debentures if interest exceeds ₹5,000 in a year (unless Form 15G/15H is validly submitted).
Capital Gains: Listed corporate bonds held for more than 12 months attract LTCG tax at 12.5% without indexation (Finance Act 2024). Short-term gains are taxed at slab rates.

sections.title: How to Buy Corporate Bonds
steps: Online Bond Platform Providers (OBPP): SEBI-regulated platforms (such as BondBazaar, Wint Wealth, GoldenPi, Grip) designed specifically for retail bond discovery.
Direct Stockbrokers: Search listed NCD symbols on NSE or BSE debt segments.
Public Issues (IPO): Apply through UPI ASBA during new corporate debenture public offerings (minimum application typically ₹10,000).

items.myth: All corporate bonds with high interest rates (12%+) are safe as long as they are listed.
items.fact: A very high yield usually reflects higher credit risk. Lower credit-rated bonds have higher default probabilities.

items.myth: Corporate bonds are insured by DICGC like bank deposits.
items.fact: Bank deposits are insured up to ₹5 lakh by DICGC; corporate bonds carry no government insurance. The investor relies on company balance sheet strength and collateral debenture trustees.

terms.definition: An independent assessment by agencies like CRISIL/ICRA evaluating the borrower's likelihood of fulfilling debt obligations.
Non-Convertible Debenture - a fixed-income debt instrument that cannot be converted into equity shares.
A SEBI-registered institution legally appointed to protect bondholders' rights and enforce security collateral in default.
